newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. refugee chief urges mass return of Bosnians.
newsitem.headline: U.N. refugee chief urges mass return of Bosnians.

text.p: The United Nations refugee chief called on Monday for a mass return of Bosnians by spring to areas where they are in the ethnic majority, but said security would have to improve before minorities could go home in 1998.

Sadako Ogata also appealed to European host countries to continue providing temporary protection to Bosnian refugees from minority areas, couples in ethnically-mixed marriages as well as former detainees and victims of extreme violence.
In a speech, she outlined her agency's priorities to a humanitarian working group, which brings together senior Balkan immigration officials with donor country representatives.
Carl Bildt, international high representative for Bosnia, as well as John Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs, were among those attending the one-day talks.
A year after the signing of the Dayton peace accord, only 250,000 of the 2.1 million Bosnians uprooted by the war have been able to return home, according to the U.N. refugee agency.
"Substantial repatriation should begin by next spring, once the harsh winter is over. In 1997 I believe that the priority will have to be on returns to majority areas," Ogata said.
"There are many who can and should now go back to rebuild their lives," she added.
"But there are other categories whose return home will depend first of all on the removal of political barriers but also on more vigorous efforts on the part of all actors on the ground.

"For the time being I must therefore urge asylum states to continue to provide protection to the following categories of refugees: first, those originating from minority areas; second, couples in mixed marriages, particularly where the head of family, upon return, would be part of a minority group; and third, special humanitarian cases such as ex-detainees and victims of extreme violence," Ogata said.

Referring to the two-year peace consolidation period of 1997-98, Ogata said: "My Office has one clear objective for the consolidation period: to ensure that all refugees and displaced persons from former Yugoslavia will have found a solution by the end of 1998 or, at least, be firmly engaged in reaching a satisfactory solution."
Angelo Gnaedinger, in charge of Western and Central Europe and the Balkans at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), echoed Ogata's views that the peace process was fragile.
"At the political level, progress is slow...Those who want to go back of their own free will should be given all necessary support, however, nobody should be compelled to do so," he said.
Some 16,000 people were reportedly still unaccounted for since the end of the 43-month war, according to the Swiss-run ICRC which runs a tracing and family reunification programme.

Nudzeim Recica, Bosnian minister for refugees and displaced persons, Bratislava Morina, Serbian commissioner for refugees, and Ljubisa Vladusic, minister for refugees and displaced persons of Republic Srpska were due to attend the Geneva talks. Croatia was being represented by Ambassador Darko Bekic.
The humanitarian meeting was to be followed by a session of the five-nation Contact Group on former Yugoslavia (Britain, France, Germany, Russia and the United States).
The political-level talks were expected to be overshadowed by growing protests in Belgrade against the cancelling of the opposition's victory in local elections last month.
Kornblum on Sunday called for Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to recognise the opposition's win in local elections, saying it was "the price" for better relations with Washington.
Kornblum also backed "democratic processes" in Serbia after more than two hours of talks with opposition leader Vuk Draskovic and other members of the Zajedno (Together) coalition.
Draskovic, who heads the Serb Renewal Movement, said he was seeking diplomatic support from the United States and European Union. He accused Milosevic of provoking violence and civil war.
